html:
Kurt Fischer’s Dynamic Skill Theory is a "skills-in-context" account of cognitive development. Instead of treating development as one global stage that applies everywhere, it says people build skills (coordinated control structures for thinking/acting) in particular domains/contexts, and those skills grow through hierarchical integration: you construct a new skill by coordinating multiple earlier skills into a single, more powerful unit. Two key consequences are (1) development looks jagged and task-dependent (you can be "advanced" in one domain and "earlier" in another), and (2) performance has a range: with support/scaffolding (which makes success barely attainable), you often show a higher "optimal" level than you show spontaneously in everyday conditions ("functional" level). For a world-modeling lens, it’s basically a theory of how internal models become more compositional, more decoupled from the here-and-now, and more rule/principle-governed over time. Fischer organizes growth into broad tiers (often described as stages): reflex -> sensorimotor actions -> representations -> abstractions. Within each tier, skills progress through four recurring, structurally identical levels: single set (agent can control one "unit" in the tier), mappings (relations between units), systems (relations between mappings), systems of systems (relations between systems; is the "single set" of the next tier). Stages and substages (similar to Case)

The below age ranges represent approximate boundaries for the child’s optimal performance (the upper limits of their abilities, which often only arise under high scaffolding (e.g., a researcher demonstrating the task, removing distractions, and explicitly prompting the child)). In everyday life (i.e without a researcher scaffolding them), children typically operate one or two levels below their optimal age. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).
